messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: matrix or array of integers?
parts:
Hi, I’m doing a logistic regression where the binary data come in matrix form, y[i,j]. Can I do this in Stan or do I need to express y as a vector?
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] matrix or array of integers?
parts:
For a 2D array of integers, that's:

int y[I,J];

But you can't use it in matrix operations. If you want
to do that you need to have

matrix[I,J] y;

But then you can't use it on the LHS of binomial or bernoulli.
If you need the binomial or bernoulli, then you are going to
need to convert the int array to a matrix in the transformed
data block.

transformed data {
matrix[I,J] y_mat;

y_mat <- to_matrix(y);
}

It's more efficient defining it once as transformed data than to
reconvert it using to_matrix() each time you need it.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] matrix or array of integers?
parts:
Key concept is the five basic types of Stan:

real-valued:
real, vector, row_vector, matrix

integer-valued:
int

Then you can have an array of any dimensionality of
any basic type.

So when you declare y as

int y[I,J];

you get a 2D integer array.

So assuming you want this:

...

for (i in 1:I)
for (j in 1:J)
y[i,j] ~ bernoulli_logit(theta);

for a fixed theta, you can do this:

to_array_1d(y) ~ bernoulli_logit(theta);

They go in column-major order (or last-index order
if the argument is more than 2D). And then theta
has to be either a single real value or an array or
vector of I*J real values.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] matrix or array of integers?
parts:
Hmm, this is tough because I fear that it destroys some simplicity in the code.

Bob,

Let me explain. First I’ll show you the linear model:

data {
int J; // #people in y
int T; // #time points in y
int K; // #parameters in delta
int K_phi; // #parameters in phi
matrix[J,T] y;
vector[T] x;
vector[K_phi] mu_phi_g; // pseudo-prior mean
cov_matrix[K_phi] Sigma_phi_g; // pseudo-prior variance
}
parameters {
matrix[J,K] eta_a;
real<lower=0> sigma_y;
vector[K] mu_a;
vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_a; // Now assuming indep
real b; // Shared parameter
}
transformed parameters {
matrix[J,K] a;
vector[K_phi] phi;
for (j in 1:J)

for (k in 1:K)
a[j,k] <- mu_a[k] + sigma_a[k]*eta_a[j,k];
phi[1] <- mu_a[1];
phi[2] <- mu_a[2];
phi[3] <- b;
phi[4] <- log(sigma_a[1]);
phi[5] <- log(sigma_a[2]);
phi[6] <- log(sigma_y);
}
model {
matrix[J,T] y_pred;
for (j in 1:J)

for (t in 1:T)
y_pred[j,t] <- a[j,1] + a[j,2]*x[t] + b*x[t]^2;
to_vector(y) ~ normal(to_vector(y_pred), sigma_y);
to_vector(eta_a) ~ normal(0,1);
phi ~ multi_normal(mu_phi_g, Sigma_phi_g);
}

You don’t really have to worry about phi here; I just included it to remind you of my desire to be able to access the concatenated transformed parameter vector directly (I need to do this because I’m running an EP-like algorithm).

Here’s the point. What I want to do is get rid of sigma_y, change the real data matrix y to an integer data array y, and replace normal by bernoulli_logit. And from your previous message it looks like I need to change to_vector to to_array_1d. But then I have a horrible feeling that the indexes will get flipped.

So maybe the best solution is to change my model and make “a” and “y_pred” into 2-way arrays instead of matrices?

This array/matrix thing is always tripping me up!

Thanks
A

what you're asking. At least not any time soon. If you want
to do matrix ops, you need to convert to a matrix (which means
real values for Stan).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] matrix or array of integers?
parts:
Did you ever end up solving your problem?  I am working on a something slightly similar and your comment "But then I have a horrible feeling that the indexes will get flipped." with some results I ran have me worried as well.

I am trying to modify some of Rob Trangucci's code for running a 2 dimensional gaussian process (see post Options for speeding up gaussian process regression). The only change I am trying to make is to change the outcome from a normal to a Poisson making it a log gaussian cox process LGCP.   I was able to change the matrix to an array but I think the indexes got flipped because when I simulated data the length scales look like they flipped their estimates.

Attached is the R code that simulates the rate data and the stan code that runs it.  Here is the r code that simulated the data, ran the stan model and the output.
## exponentiated quadratic covariance matrix function
cov_exp_quad <- function(x, alpha, len_scale, jitter) {
  dim_x = length(x)
  cov_ret <- matrix(NA_real_, dim_x, dim_x)
  for (i in 1:(dim_x - 1)) {
    cov_ret[i, i] = alpha ^ 2 + jitter
    for (j in (i + 1):dim_x) {
      r_x = (x[i] - x[j])^2
      cov_ret[i, j] = alpha^2 * exp(-1 / (2 * len_scale^2) * r_x)
      cov_ret[j,i] = cov_ret[i, j]
    }
  }
  cov_ret[dim_x, dim_x] = alpha ^ 2 + jitter
  return(cov_ret)
}

## DGP

set.seed(320)

dim_x_1 <- 100
dim_x_2 <- 100
alpha <- 0.5
len_scale_x_1 <- 4
len_scale_x_2 <- 2

x_1 <- seq(0,20,length.out = dim_x_1)
x_2 <- seq(0,20,length.out = dim_x_2)
cov_mat_x_1 <- cov_exp_quad(x_1, 1.0, len_scale_x_1, 1e-12)
cov_mat_x_2 <- cov_exp_quad(x_2, alpha, len_scale_x_2, 1e-12)
L_x_1 <- t(chol(cov_mat_x_1))
L_x_2 <- t(chol(cov_mat_x_2))
y_tilde <- matrix(rnorm(dim_x_1 * dim_x_2),dim_x_1,dim_x_2)
gp_draw <- L_x_1 %*% y_tilde %*% t(L_x_2)

mu <- exp(gp_draw + matrix(0.5 * rnorm(dim_x_1 * dim_x_2), dim_x_1, dim_x_2))

y <- matrix(NA, nrow=100, ncol=100)
for (i in 1:100) {

 y[i,] <-rpois(100,mu[i,1:100]) 
}


## Generate data to pass to Stan model

stan_dat <- list(y = y,
                 N = prod(dim(y)),
                 dim_x_1 = dim_x_1,
                 dim_x_2 = dim_x_2,
                 x_1 = x_1,
                 x_2 = x_2)

fit <- stan('lgcp_2dim_ncp.stan', data = stan_dat, chains = 4, iter = 3000, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95, max_treedepth = 15), cores = 4)

samps <- rstan::extract(fit)

print(fit, pars = c('alpha','len_scale_x_1','len_scale_x_2'))

Thanks for any help you can provide!!
-Patrick

On Sunday, May 10, 2015 at 4:11:19 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
Hmm, this is tough because I fear that it destroys some simplicity in the code.

Bob,

Let me explain.  First I’ll show you the linear model:

data {
  int J;                         // #people in y
  int T;                         // #time points in y
  int K;                         // #parameters in delta
  int K_phi;                     // #parameters in phi
  matrix[J,T] y;
  vector[T] x;
  vector[K_phi] mu_phi_g;        // pseudo-prior mean
  cov_matrix[K_phi] Sigma_phi_g; // pseudo-prior variance
}
parameters {
  matrix[J,K] eta_a;
  real<lower=0> sigma_y;
  vector[K] mu_a;
  vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_a;    // Now assuming indep
  real b;                        // Shared parameter
}
transformed parameters {
  matrix[J,K] a;
  vector[K_phi] phi;
  for (j in 1:J)
    for (k in 1:K)
      a[j,k] <- mu_a[k] + sigma_a[k]*eta_a[j,k];
  phi[1] <- mu_a[1];
  phi[2] <- mu_a[2];
  phi[3] <- b;
  phi[4] <- log(sigma_a[1]);
  phi[5] <- log(sigma_a[2]);
  phi[6] <- log(sigma_y);
}
model {
  matrix[J,T] y_pred;
  for (j in 1:J)
    for (t in 1:T)
      y_pred[j,t] <- a[j,1] + a[j,2]*x[t] + b*x[t]^2;
  to_vector(y) ~ normal(to_vector(y_pred), sigma_y);
  to_vector(eta_a) ~ normal(0,1);
  phi ~ multi_normal(mu_phi_g, Sigma_phi_g);
}

You don’t really have to worry about phi here; I just included it to remind you of my desire to be able to access the concatenated transformed parameter vector directly (I need to do this because I’m running an EP-like algorithm).

Here’s the point.  What I want to do is get rid of sigma_y, change the real data matrix y to an integer data array y, and replace normal by bernoulli_logit.  And from your previous message it looks like I need to change to_vector to to_array_1d.  But then I have a horrible feeling that the indexes will get flipped.

So maybe the best solution is to change my model and make “a” and “y_pred” into 2-way arrays instead of matrices?

This array/matrix thing is always tripping me up!

Thanks
A

> Key concept is the five basic types of Stan:
>
>  real-valued:
>    real, vector, row_vector, matrix
>
>  integer-valued:
>    int
>
> Then you can have an array of any dimensionality of
> any basic type.  
>
> So when you declare y as
>
>  int y[I,J];
>
> you get a 2D integer array.  
>
> So assuming you want this:
>
> ...
>
>  for (i in 1:I)
>    for (j in 1:J)
>      y[i,j] ~ bernoulli_logit(theta);
>
> for a fixed theta, you can do this:
>
>  to_array_1d(y) ~ bernoulli_logit(theta);
>
> They go in column-major order (or last-index order

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] matrix or array of integers?
parts:
You have to be careful with the ordering of columns vs. rows
in all of the conversion operators. Underlyingly, our matrices
are column major (Eigen C++ library default) and our arrays are
row major (using standard C++ library vector). So it's always
confusing going back and forth between them, in both the I/O
and the internal functions.

You can write a program with just generated quantities and
run it to do simple testing to make sure you have things in
the right order.

- Bob
